name: Pitch tracking apps

lead: Pitch tracking apps listen to your voice and report its fundamental frequency, usually in hertz or as a note name. They are used to check speaking pitch.
No clinical research evaluates them for appearance or voice-change goals; sources describe only the general technology.

paras: They apply pitch detection algorithms such as autocorrelation, YIN or spectral methods to estimate the period of the voice signal and convert it to frequency.
No direct harms are documented. Documented technical limits include octave errors and noise sensitivity, so readings may be inaccurate.

lead: Pitch tracking apps are smartphone or desktop programs that estimate the fundamental frequency (f0) of a recorded or live voice and display it in hertz or as a musical note. In voice-related appearance and presentation communities they are used to check how high or low a speaking voice sits, for example when practising a deeper or more resonant voice.[1][2]

Pitch is the listener's subjective impression of how high or low a sound is, while fundamental frequency is the measurable lowest repetition rate of a periodic sound; the two track each other closely but are not identical.[1] Apps typically apply a pitch detection algorithm, a family of methods that estimate the period of a quasi-periodic signal such as speech and invert it to a frequency.[2]

Published sources on these apps as a product category are thin, and no clinical study of a specific looksmaxxing-oriented pitch app was found. The description below therefore covers the underlying technology and its documented limits.
infobox: Fundamental frequency (f0), in Hz or note names
Autocorrelation, YIN, MPM, cepstral and spectral methods[2]
Consumer software; not a medical device unless marketed as one

paras: Pitch detection algorithms estimate the period of a nearly periodic waveform and convert it to frequency. Time-domain approaches include autocorrelation-style methods and refinements such as YIN and MPM, while frequency-domain approaches use spectra, cepstral analysis or harmonic product spectrum. Hybrid methods combine both.[2]

Documented limitations include octave errors, where the detector locks onto an overtone rather than the true fundamental, sensitivity to noise, and a trade-off in window length for low voices, since speech fundamentals span roughly 40 to 600 Hz and low pitches need longer analysis windows during which pitch may change.[2]

Adult male vocal folds are longer (about 17 to 25 mm) than female ones (about 12.5 to 17.5 mm), which is associated with lower male pitch.[3] Voice therapy is used by some trans people to adjust pitch and resonance, and sessions are often recorded to provide auditory feedback.[4]

Within voice-improvement discussions, practitioners describe using such apps to see their average speaking pitch and track changes after practice. No published study evaluates this use in that community.
